```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
set.seed(11)

# Small real examples from the instructional dataset.
dat <- "../../../datasets/2-workshop2/instructional_dataset"
mb <- read_csv(file.path(dat, "02_microbiome_counts.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
rn <- read_csv(file.path(dat, "04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
genes <- read_csv(file.path(dat, "05_gene_annotation.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(ensembl_gene_id, symbol)
top_share <- function(m) {
  x <- as.matrix(m[, -1])
  tibble(sample = colnames(x), share = apply(x, 2, max) / colSums(x))
}
dominance <- bind_rows(species = top_share(mb), genes = top_share(rn), .id = "table") |>
  mutate(table = factor(table, c("species", "genes")))
```

## This afternoon {.center}

We won't run any software today.

. . .

By the end of the afternoon you should be able to explain, in your own words,
where each number in a count table came from.

## A sequencer returns text

```
@A00984:412:HTKJ7DSXX:1:1101:2645:1000 1:N:0:ACTGAGCG
TACGTAGGGTGCGAGCGTTGTCCGGATTTATTGGGCGTAAAGCGCGCGCAGGCGGTTTGTT
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFF
```

. . .

Each sample produces millions of these records: a read name, the sequence, and
a quality score for every base.

. . .

All the processing after this tries to answer **what was in the tube, and how
much of it?**

## Not every base is trustworthy

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.3
set.seed(7)
tibble(cycle = 1:150) |>
  mutate(q = 38 - 0.00035 * cycle^2 - rnorm(150, 0, 0.4),
         lo = q - 4.5, hi = pmin(q + 2.5, 41)) |>
  ggplot(aes(cycle, q)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = pal[["teal"]], alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["navy"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = 2, colour = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 17.5, label = "a common trimming threshold",
           size = 4.2, colour = pal[["orange"]], hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "position in the read", y = "quality score") +
  ylim(10, 42)
```

Quality drops toward the end of each read. Before any counting, someone trimmed
off the low-quality ends.

## The decisions already made for you

By the time you receive a count table, someone has chosen:

::: {.incremental}
- where to trim each read
- which samples were too poor to keep
- which reference to compare against
- what to do with reads that matched more than one thing
- what to do with reads that matched nothing
:::

. . .

You won't find these choices in the table, but each one changed its numbers, so
ask who made them.

## Both pipelines end in a count table

```{r}
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 6.4
steps <- tribble(
  ~path, ~step, ~label,
  "16S", 1, "cervico-\nvaginal\nswab",
  "16S", 2, "amplify\n16S V3-V4",
  "16S", 3, "sequence",
  "16S", 4, "denoise\ninto exact\nsequences",
  "16S", 5, "classify\nagainst a\nreference",
  "16S", 6, "counts per\nspecies",
  "RNA", 1, "cervico-\nvaginal\nswab",
  "RNA", 2, "capture\nmRNA, make\ncDNA",
  "RNA", 3, "sequence",
  "RNA", 4, "align to\nthe human\ngenome",
  "RNA", 5, "count reads\nper gene\nmodel",
  "RNA", 6, "counts per\ngene"
) |>
  mutate(y = if_else(path == "16S", 2, 1),
         fill = case_when(step == 6 ~ pal[["navy"]],
                          path == "16S" ~ pal[["teal"]],
                          TRUE ~ pal[["orange"]]))

ggplot(steps, aes(step, y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = step, xend = step + 0.98, y = y, yend = y),
               data = steps |> filter(step < 6),
               colour = pal[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.8,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = fill), width = 0.92, height = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), colour = "white", size = 6.6, lineheight = 0.9,
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(2, 1), labels = c("16S", "RNA-seq"), limits = c(0.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 20) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey25", hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(r = 10)))
```

The lab work and the software differ at every step. Both end with features in
rows, samples in columns, and read counts in the cells.

## 16S: one gene, every bacterium

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
The 16S ribosomal RNA gene is in every bacterium, and parts of it differ between
species.

::: {.incremental}
- amplify one variable region with PCR
- sequence only that amplicon
- group identical sequences together
- look each one up in a reference database
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(conserved = 0.15 + 0.1 * sin(x * 3),
         variable = if_else(x > 3 & x < 5 | x > 7 & x < 8.5, 0.9, 0.15)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x)) +
  geom_area(aes(y = variable), fill = pal[["teal"]], alpha = 0.85) +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 1.05, label = "V3", size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.75, y = 1.05, label = "V4", size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.36, label = "conserved", size = 5, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "position along the 16S gene", y = "variation between species") +
  ylim(0, 1.15) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## PCR distorts the proportions

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(
  species = c("species A", "species B", "species C", "species D"),
  truth = c(40, 30, 20, 10),
  observed = c(26, 41, 11, 22)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-species, names_to = "what", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, truth = "cells in the tube", observed = "reads you get back")) |>
  ggplot(aes(species, pct, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`cells in the tube` = pal[["grey"]],
                               `reads you get back` = pal[["teal"]])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "percent", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Primers bind some templates better than others, and 16S copy number varies
between species, so the most common species in the reads may not be the most
common in the tube.

## Grouping reads: ASVs and OTUs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
If two reads differ by one base, did they come from one organism or two?

::: {.incremental}
- **OTUs** cluster anything within some cutoff of each other, say 3%. Errors get
  absorbed, and so do close relatives.
- **ASVs** model the sequencing error process and keep exact sequences. They can
  separate close relatives, if the error model is right.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(12)
tibble(x = c(rnorm(60, 2, 0.35), rnorm(40, 4, 0.35), rnorm(8, 3, 1.2)),
       y = c(rnorm(60, 2, 0.35), rnorm(40, 3.4, 0.35), rnorm(8, 2.6, 1.2)),
       kind = c(rep("abundant variant", 60), rep("abundant variant", 40),
                rep("error reads", 8))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = kind, size = kind)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`abundant variant` = pal[["navy"]],
                                 `error reads` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(3, 1.8)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  theme_void(base_size = 18) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

## Classification often stops short of species

The sequenced region is short, and some species are identical across it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  `what the classifier can say` = c("Lactobacillus crispatus",
                                    "Gardnerella, but which species is ambiguous",
                                    "family only",
                                    "bacteria"),
  `how our table names it` = c("lactobacillus_crispatus",
                              "gardnerella_swidsinskii_leopoldii",
                              "prevotella_sp_1",
                              "dropped")
) |> knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Two of our 220 row names admit this uncertainty in the name itself, so read the
row names before you interpret them.

## A 16S count is a number of reads

A cell in the species table is **the number of amplicon reads in this sample
that matched this species.**

. . .

It is not the number of bacteria. The count also depends on

::: {.incremental}
- how many copies of the 16S gene that species carries
- how well the primers bind to it
- how completely the cells lysed
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## RNA-seq: every gene, one organism

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental}
- pull out messenger RNA
- copy it to cDNA and fragment it
- sequence the fragments
- find where each fragment belongs in the genome
- count fragments overlapping each gene
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
reads <- tibble(start = runif(26, 0, 9), y = rep(1:13, each = 2) * 0.07 + 0.25)
tibble(x = 0) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["grey"]]) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(1, 4.2, 7.5), xmax = c(2.6, 6, 9.2), ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["navy"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.8, y = -0.01, label = "exon", size = 5, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_segment(data = reads, aes(x = start, xend = start + 0.75, y = y, yend = y),
               colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "position along the gene", y = NULL) +
  xlim(0, 10) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## An RNA-seq count is a number of fragments

A cell in the gene table is **the number of fragments in this sample assigned
to this gene.**

. . .

It is not the number of mRNA molecules either. The count also depends on

::: {.incremental}
- how long the gene is
- how well the capture chemistry worked
- whether the read could be placed uniquely
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## One swab, two experiments

A cervicovaginal swab contains human cells and bacteria together.

::: {.incremental}
- The 16S run amplifies a bacterial gene, so human material is mostly ignored.
- The RNA-seq run captures polyadenylated RNA, which is mostly human.
- Neither table is pure, but both come from the same swab.
:::

. . .

Because they share a swab, we can pair the two tables sample by sample.

## The two tables share their columns {.smaller}

```{r}
show_ids <- c("P001_week_18", "P001_week_24", "P002_week_18")
peek <- function(m, label, what) {
  names(m)[1] <- "feature"
  m |>
    select(feature, all_of(show_ids)) |>
    mutate(total = rowSums(across(all_of(show_ids)))) |>
    slice_max(total, n = 4) |>
    select(-total) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(show_ids), ~ scales::comma(.x))) |>
    add_row(feature = paste("...", scales::comma(nrow(m) - 4), "more", what)) |>
    mutate(table = c(label, rep("", n() - 1)), .before = 1)
}
bind_rows(
  peek(mb, "16S", "species"),
  rn |>
    left_join(genes, by = "ensembl_gene_id") |>
    select(symbol, everything(), -ensembl_gene_id) |>
    peek('<span style="white-space: nowrap">RNA-seq</span>', "genes")
) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(.x, ""))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("table", "row", show_ids), align = "llrrr")
```

The rows with the most reads, in the first three columns of each table. Every
sample ID is a column in both tables, so any sample can be looked up in both.

## Some reads fit more than one gene

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(x = 0) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(0.5, 5.5), xmax = c(3.5, 8.5), ymin = 1, ymax = 1.5,
           fill = pal[["navy"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = c(2, 7), y = 1.75, label = c("gene A", "gene B"), size = 4.6) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.3, xmax = 4.9, ymin = 0.45, ymax = 0.75,
           fill = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.6, y = 0.2, label = "one read, two homes", size = 4.4,
           colour = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.6, xend = c(2.6, 6.6), y = 0.8, yend = 0.95,
           colour = pal[["orange"]], linetype = 2) +
  xlim(0, 9) + ylim(0, 2) +
  theme_void()
```

Gene families and repeated sequences produce reads that match several genes
equally well. Counting such a read once, twice, or not at all gives a different
table each time.

## Counts, not TPM, for testing {.smaller}

You will see expression reported as TPM, FPKM or RPKM. Those divide by gene
length so you can compare genes within a sample.

::: {.incremental}
- Good for: "is gene A higher than gene B in this sample?"
- Wrong for: the statistical tests we run on Tuesday
:::

. . .

Those tests need raw counts, because they model counting noise. Hand them
normalised values and they will believe the noise is smaller than it is.

. . .

```{r}
tibble(sample = c("sample 1", "sample 2"),
       library = c(2e6, 20e6),
       reads = c(10, 100)) |>
  mutate(per_million = reads / library * 1e6,
         lo = qpois(0.025, reads) / library * 1e6,
         hi = qpois(0.975, reads) / library * 1e6,
         `reads for gene X` = reads,
         `library size` = scales::comma(library),
         `reads per million` = per_million,
         `range if sequenced again` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", lo, hi)) |>
  select(sample, `library size`, `reads for gene X`, `reads per million`,
         `range if sequenced again`) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The normalised values match. Only the raw counts show that sample 1 rests on
ten reads.

## When C grows, A and B appear to shrink

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5.2
d <- tibble(
  sample = rep(c("sample 1", "sample 2"), each = 3),
  feature = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), 2),
  absolute = c(100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 700)
) |>
  group_by(sample) |>
  mutate(relative = absolute / sum(absolute)) |>
  ungroup()

p_abs <- ggplot(d, aes(sample, absolute, fill = feature)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "what is really there", x = NULL, y = "cells") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("teal", "navy", "orange")]))
p_rel <- ggplot(d, aes(sample, relative, fill = feature)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "what the count table shows", x = NULL, y = "share of reads") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("teal", "navy", "orange")]))
p_abs + p_rel + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

A and B have 100 cells in both samples, but their share of the reads falls from
a third to a ninth.

## Both of our tables are compositional

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- 16S is hit hardest, because one species routinely holds 90% of the reads.
- RNA-seq is affected less, since no single gene dominates, but the effect is
  still there.
:::

"Relative abundance went down" and "there was less of it" are different claims.
Without a spike-in or an absolute measurement, you cannot tell them apart.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.2
ggplot(dominance, aes(table, share, colour = table)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(size = 1.3, alpha = 0.7, width = 0.38) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(species = pal[["teal"]], genes = pal[["orange"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(species = "16S species", genes = "RNA-seq genes")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "reads held by the top feature",
       title = "one dot per sample, our 471 samples") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 15, colour = "grey35"))
```
:::
::::

## Ask your sequencing facility for

::: {.incremental}
- the raw reads, not just the table
- the exact reference and version used
- which samples failed and were re-run
- which plate, run and lane each sample sat on
- the negative and positive controls, with their counts
:::

. . .

The controls are how you catch contamination, and few people ask for them.

## Common problems and how to spot them

| problem | how you notice |
|---|---|
| contamination from reagents | the same taxa in your negative controls |
| low-biomass samples | tiny library sizes, odd composition |
| index hopping between samples | a trace of everything in everything |
| a batch effect | samples cluster by run, not by biology |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

. . .

You can only see three of these four if somebody recorded the metadata.

## The sentence to remember {.center}

A count measures how much of something was in the tube **relative to everything
else in that tube**, multiplied by how hard we looked.

## Every analysis starts the same way

::: {.incremental}
1. How deeply was each sample sequenced?
2. Which features are we even able to see?
3. Only then: does anything differ between groups?
:::

. . .

Tomorrow morning covers the first two, on both tables at once.

## Our gene table has a batch label

The gene table was produced in **two sequencing batches**, and we kept that
label in the metadata.

. . .

On Wednesday you will measure how much of the table the batch explains, and
the answer is uncomfortable.

. . .

Keep every technical label your sequencing facility gives you. A batch effect
you never recorded is one you cannot test for.

## On your feet {.center}

Put the laptops away.

. . .

For the next ninety minutes we build count tables by hand.
